newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian auto workers reach pact with Chrysler.
newsitem.headline: Canadian auto workers reach pact with Chrysler.

text.p: The Canadian Auto Workers and Chrysler Corp. Canada sealed a new labor agreement on Tuesday covering 12,600 workers, narrowly averting a strike deadline.

CAW President Buzz Hargrove said the deal avoided many of the concessions that the unit of the Detroit-based automaker was seeking, including over the crucial issue of outsourcing work to non-union shops.
The agreement with Chrysler, due to be ratified by workers on Sunday, will also set the pattern of bargaining ahead with the Canadian subsidiaries of Ford Motor Co. and General Motors Corp.

"I am pleased to announce that we have a tentative agreement that has just received unanimous approval of the Chrysler bargaining committee for our 1996 negotiations with Chrysler Canada, which will establish the pattern for the auto industry in Canada," Hargrove said.
The Canadian agreement comes on the heals of a U.S. deal on Monday between the United Auto Workers and Ford Motor Co., which covered 105,000 hourly workers.
Hargrove said the Canadian union on Monday will announce the target of its next negotiations.
Chrysler Canada officials said the company was relieved the agreement was reached without a strike. The deal was announced just 1-1/2 hours before the union contract was due to expire at midnight.

"The fact is now we can concentrate on the thing we do best and that is building cars and trucks which people enjoy buying," said Chrysler Canada spokesman Othmar Stein. "It's a relief ... we're pleased we could accomplish this without resulting in a strike."

The union said the agreement included a 2-percent wage increase in each year of a three-year settlement, improved the health care plan, and avoided giving in to Chrysler's demands for user fees, co-payments and caps on the health and benefit plans for union workers.
"All of the concessions that the company had on the table have been succesfully removed and improvements have been made in many areas in our health care plan," Hargrove said.
Although the union said the improvement in health care benefits did not come at the expense of wage increases, Chrysler's Stein suggested some horse-trading had occurred.
"Well there are always tradeoffs," Stein said. "I mean negotiations -- as I say, it's the art of the compromise."

A strike-averting deal began to look possible after both sides announced late on Monday that they had come to an agreement on the critical issue of outsourcing. Outsourcing is the sale of plants or transfer of work to outside contractors whose employees generally are not members of auto unions.
The union said the pact will limit Chrysler's outsourcing and place a virtual embargo on the sale or closure of any profitable plants during the life of the three-year deal.
Chrysler officials said the deal also satisfies its own concerns in a changing market.
"During the terms of this agreement there won't be major outsourcing, but it still gives us flexibility in certain areas as long as we're in discussions with the CAW," Stein said.
The union vowed early on Tuesday to extend its agreement with Chrysler on limiting outsourcing when it confronts General Motors of Canada and Ford Canada at the bargaining table.
GM Canada has said it intends to sell two plants in Canada and outsource more than 5,000 jobs.
